newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Volunteers mount on new force for Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Volunteers mount on new force for Zaire.

text.p: With the United Nations close to approving an international force for eastern Zaire, officials on Thursday were scrambling to complete plans that would get troops to the region to feed over a million refugees.

Troop contributing countries and other delegations for the planned intervention force were holding a series of meetings with Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril of Canada, who will lead the force, and other officials in an effort to define its mandate.

At least 10,000 foreign troops eventually were expected in the region but the initial force would include soldiers from the United States, Canada, Britain, France, Spain, Italy, the Netherlands, South Africa and Senegal, diplomats said.

A fund is expected to set up for other African nations such as Cameroon, Ethiopia, Eritrea and others. In addition envoys said Egypt, Belgium, Ireland, Brazil and Portugal have volunteered troops and Norway and Finland may send human rights observers.
To encourage Hutu refugees in eastern Zaire to return home to Rwanda, the United Nations has suggested human rights monitors in Rwanda be increased from 110 to about 300, the diplomats added.
Still unclear are the rules of engagement and what the force would do if caught in the fighting between Tutsis who have lived in Zaire for over 100 years and the Zairean army.

The United States, which will field up to 1,000 soldiers in eastern Zaire and up to 4,000 more in various neighbouring countries, also wants humanitarian corridors to encourage Hutu refugees to return to Rwanda. U.S. troops are expected to be around Goma in the northern part of Zaire's Kivu province while French and British troops may be at Bukavu airport in the southern part of the province, U.N. sources said.

Canada, which will take the lead in the operation, was expected to write a letter to the U.N. Security Council shortly outlining the concept for the force. But the 15-member council was not expected to endorse the force before Friday, depending whether members were satisfied with the plans.

On hand for some sessions will be White House National Security Adviser Anthony Lake, Defence Undersecretary Walter Slocombe and Air Force Lt. Gen. Peter Pace, who is director of operations for the Joint Chiefs of Staff.

About 1.5 million refugees, mainly Hutus, fled Rwanda in 1994, fearing reprisals after the massacre of up to a million Tutsis and Hutu moderates. The eastern Zairean province of Kivu has remained politically tense since then, with a new war breaking out in September between Tutsi residents of Zaire and local Zaireans backed by Zaire's rag-tag army.

The international force would remain no longer than six months after which some troops may stay on under a U.N. peacekeeping umbrella. The current operation was being organised outside of the United Nations but endorsed by it.
But there were signs already that the force would meet resistance as relief teams, including those from the U.S. Agency for International Development, have been turned back.

Unclear also was how feeding centres would be organised for the refugees without duplicating the current camps, used as bases by the former Hutu army chased out of Rwanda when the Tutsis two years ago took control of the government.
"This operation by its very nature is a humanitarian one and the international community is not going in to start a war," said U.N. spokesman Ahmad Fawzi.

"They are going to go in there and try and separate the militia from the real refugees. When you come to be fed you don't need a gun," he said. "Some very useful ideas have been put forward on how to achieve separation without confrontation."
